problem: Generative retrieval methods rely on trie-constrained beam search, making them vulnerable to early pruning of relevant prefixes under finite-beam decoding (prefix pruning), which Planning Ahead in Generative Retrieval (PAG) aims to mitigate by using simultaneous decoding to compute a document-level look-ahead prior (p.1-2).
methodology: The study reproduces PAG at inference time using released artifacts and stress-tests its decoding behavior under intent-preserving query variations (misspellings, reordering, synonyms, paraphrases, and naturality shifts) and fixed-index cross-lingual query shift using non-English mMARCO queries against an English index (p.1, 2). It introduces plan drift diagnostics (such as CandOverlap@K, TokJaccard@l, planning-only retrieval change, counterfactual plan swap, and guided decoding gain) to quantify planning stability and collapse, and evaluates query-side mitigations like query translation and planner-token distillation (p.3-5).
dataset: MS MARCO Dev (6,980 queries), TREC-DL 2019/2020, and non-English mMARCO query sets (Chinese, Dutch, French, and German) evaluated against the English MS MARCO passage collection (8.8M passages) (p.5, 6).
results: Reproduced PAG matches reported MRR@10 and NDCG@10 effectiveness values within 0.002 absolute difference on MS MARCO Dev and TREC-DL 2019/2020 at the default setting (k=100, m=64), corroborating the reported beam-size-latency trade-off (p.1, 5, 6). However, PAG's planning signal is brittle under lexical surface-form variation and cross-lingual shifts, where intent-preserving typos and language mismatch can trigger plan collapse and weaken guided decoding (p.1, 2, 7-10).
key_findings: PAG's reported effectiveness and the benefits of planning-guided decoding are validated under the released inference setup, but these gains depend heavily on the stability of the planning signal (p.1, 2). Intent-preserving query variations can cause plan collapse—shifting the planned candidate pool enough that the look-ahead bonus provides little useful guidance and reverts decoding toward weaker unguided search (p.1, 2). For cross-lingual query shift with a fixed English index, query-only translation provides substantially stronger recovery than lightweight planner-token distillation without re-indexing (p.1, 2, 6, 11).
title: Lost in Decoding? Reproducing and Stress-Testing the Look-Ahead Prior in Generative Retrieval
